deep.reconstruction:
This is a short scratch page. It sets up the theta-function (Mellin transform) proof of the functional equation of zeta, and derives the needed Gaussian Fourier integral. Riemann's notation: Pi(s) = Gamma(s+1).

(1) Mellin integral of a Gaussian term. The page writes
Pi(s/2-1) n^{-s} pi^{-s/2} = int_0^oo e^{-n^2 pi x} x^{s/2-1} dx.
In modern terms, Gamma(s/2) (pi n^2)^{-s/2} = int_0^oo e^{-pi n^2 x} x^{s/2-1} dx. This follows from substituting u = pi n^2 x in the Gamma integral.
Summing over n (my completion of the struck line) gives
zeta(s) pi^{-s/2} Pi(s/2-1) = Pi(s/2-1) pi^{-s/2} sum_{n>=1} n^{-s} = int_0^oo psi(x) x^{s/2-1} dx,
where psi(x) = sum_{n>=1} e^{-n^2 pi x}. This is the starting identity of the second proof in the 1859 paper. The isolated note 'e^{-nn pi x}' marks psi as the object to be transformed.

(2) Gaussian integrals.
- Pi(-1/2) = int_{-oo}^{oo} e^{-y^2} dy, i.e. Gamma(1/2) = sqrt(pi).
- Scaling y -> sqrt(beta) y gives beta^{-1/2} Pi(-1/2) = int e^{-beta y^2} dy.
- Completing the square, -beta y^2 + 2 beta alpha i y = -beta (y - alpha i)^2 - beta alpha^2.
- Shifting the line of integration (implicit Cauchy argument, my addition) gives beta^{-1/2} Pi(-1/2) = e^{beta alpha^2} int e^{-beta y^2 + 2 beta alpha i y} dy.

(3) Specialisation. Put beta = pi x and alpha = -n:
int_{-oo}^{oo} e^{-pi x y^2 - 2 pi n x i y} dy = (pi x)^{-1/2} Pi(-1/2) e^{-n^2 pi x} = x^{-1/2} e^{-pi n^2 x}.

(4) Second version, by the saddle-point method. The page next writes e^{-pi x y^2 - 2 n pi i y} dy, apparently without x in the linear term.
- The stationary point of the exponent solves 2 pi x y + 2 pi n i = 0, so y = -n i / x. Riemann writes y = ni/x.
- The page then writes e^{-pi (y - ni/x)...}, shorthand for e^{-pi x (y + ni/x)^2}, and a residual factor e^{... pi n^2 / x}.
- My completion: the exponent is -pi x y^2 - 2 pi n i y = -pi x (y + n i/x)^2 - pi n^2/x.
- Hence int e^{-pi x y^2 - 2 pi n i y} dy = x^{-1/2} e^{-pi n^2/x}. This is the Fourier transform of e^{-pi x y^2} at frequency n.
- Summing over all integers n with Poisson summation (not written on the page) gives the theta transformation sum_n e^{-pi n^2/x} = sqrt(x) sum_n e^{-pi n^2 x}, i.e. 2 psi(1/x) + 1 = sqrt(x) (2 psi(x) + 1). This is exactly the identity Riemann uses in 1859.

(5) Pencil arithmetic at the bottom. These are unrelated column sums, e.g. 709 + 605 = 1314, 1314 + 370 = 1684, 5 + 30 + 70 + 200 ... = 300-odd. They look like household or accounting sums with no mathematical content.

Context: the facing pages hold Riemann–Siegel-type asymptotic work (previous page) and Mellin/Perron-type integrals for log zeta (next page). This page is a reminder derivation of the theta/Gaussian ingredients.
errors: The first specialised integral keeps x in the linear term (-2 pi n x i y). It is correct as written, with value x^{-1/2} e^{-pi n^2 x}, but it is not the form needed for the theta inversion. The following line switches to -2 n pi i y, which is the useful form.
The stationary point is written y = ni/x. For the exponent -pi x y^2 - 2 n pi i y it should be y = -ni/x. This is a sign slip, or an alternative sign convention in the linear term.
In 'e^{-pi(y - ni/x)}' the square and the factor x in the exponent are omitted (shorthand).

The residual factor appears as e^{+pi nn/x}. On the integral side it should be e^{-pi n^2/x}; the + sign is correct only if the factor has been moved to the other side, as with e^{+beta alpha alpha} earlier on the page.
The contour shift that justifies completing the square with an imaginary shift is not stated (routine).

results.what: Gamma(s/2) pi^{-s/2} n^{-s} = int_0^oo e^{-pi n^2 x} x^{s/2-1} dx, hence pi^{-s/2} Gamma(s/2) zeta(s) = int_0^oo psi(x) x^{s/2-1} dx
results.modern_name: Mellin transform representation of the completed zeta function (theta-function method)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1859 (second proof of the functional equation)

results.what: int e^{-beta y^2 + 2 beta alpha i y} dy = sqrt(pi/beta) e^{-beta alpha^2}; in particular int e^{-pi x y^2 - 2 pi n i y} dy = x^{-1/2} e^{-pi n^2/x}
results.modern_name: Fourier transform of a Gaussian (completing the square / saddle point)

results.what: Implied use toward the theta inversion sum e^{-pi n^2/x} = sqrt(x) sum e^{-pi n^2 x}
results.modern_name: Jacobi theta transformation via Poisson summation
results.usually_credited_to: Jacobi (1828), Poisson, Cauchy; used by Riemann 1859

deep.surprise_reason: The page re-derives the standard Gaussian Fourier transform needed for the theta-function proof of the zeta functional equation. Riemann published that proof in 1859, so nothing here goes beyond known material.

checkable.asserts: Gamma(s/2)(pi n^2)^{-s/2} = int_0^oo e^{-pi n^2 x} x^{s/2-1} dx
beta^{-1/2} Pi(-1/2) = int e^{-beta y^2} dy
completing the square: e^{beta alpha^2} int e^{-beta y^2+2 beta alpha i y} dy = beta^{-1/2} Pi(-1/2)
the specialised integral on the page equals (pi x)^{-1/2} Pi(-1/2) e^{-n^2 pi x}
Fourier transform of e^{-pi x y^2} at n is x^{-1/2} e^{-pi n^2/x} (saddle at y=-ni/x)
theta inversion sum e^{-pi n^2/x} = sqrt(x) sum e^{-pi n^2 x} (numerically ~0 at x=3/2)

transcription_corrections: Line 2: the struck exponent is -s; the intended left side reads Pi(s/2-1) n^{-s} pi^{-s/2}.
The second Gaussian integrand appears to read e^{-pi x yy - 2 n pi i y} (no x in the linear term), not a repeat of the earlier e^{-pi x yy - 2 pi n x i y}.
The stationary-point line is better read as '2 pi x y - 2 n pi i = 0' (or '2xy - 2ni = 0' after cancelling pi); the transcription '2xy - 2nxi = 0' is doubtful.
'e e^{+pi nn/x}' is partly struck; it is the residual factor exp(±pi n^2/x) from completing the square.
The pencil numbers bottom left are unrelated arithmetic, partly struck. The legible column sums are 709+605=1314 and 1314+370=1684; the reading '1684' is supported by the sum.
